props.title: Scanners
props.initialSlug: Psychics wage war with explosive mental powers

sections.content: David Cronenberg's Scanners (1981) revolutionized body horror with its explosive blend of psychological thriller and grotesque practical effects. The infamous head explosion scene remains one of cinema's most shocking practical effects achievements, created using actual explosives and a gelatin head filled with dog food and fake blood. The film established Cronenberg's signature style of combining visceral body horror with deeper philosophical questions, much like his earlier work The Brood (1979) and later masterpiece Videodrome (1983).

sections.content: The film's exploration of psychic powers and corporate exploitation predated similar themes in later sci-fi horror hybrids like Akira (1988) and The Fury (1978). Michael Ironside's performance as the villainous Darryl Revok set a new standard for telekinetic antagonists, influencing characters in everything from Chronicle (2012) to Push (2009). The film's practical effects work by Dick Smith and Gary Zeller pushed boundaries that would influence decades of horror cinema.

Cronenberg's clinical approach to body horror in Scanners marked a significant evolution from earlier exploitation films. While movies like Carrie (1976) used telekinesis as a metaphor for puberty and social alienation, Scanners frames psychic abilities through the lens of pharmaceutical manipulation and corporate warfare - themes that would later appear in films like Inception (2010) and Lucy (2014). sections.content: The film spawned several sequels, though none matched the original's impact. Its influence extends beyond horror into mainstream sci-fi, with films like District 9 (2009) and Looper (2012) borrowing its mix of corporate conspiracy and body transformation. The practical effects revolution it helped spark continued through films like The Thing (1982) and The Fly (1986), another Cronenberg masterpiece.
